An adnexal mass is an abnormal swelling or lesion involving structures adjacent to the uterus, particularly:
The ovary.
The fallopian tube.
The broad ligament and surrounding tissues.
Adjacent pelvic structures that may mimic an adnexal lesion.
Adnexal masses may be physiological, benign, borderline or malignant.
Follicular cysts and corpus luteum cysts are common in reproductive-age women. Many resolve spontaneously.
Associated with endometriosis and often appears as a cyst with homogeneous low-level internal echoes on ultrasound.
A benign germ cell tumour that may contain fat, hair or calcified material. It can predispose to ovarian torsion.
May contain solid areas, papillary projections, irregular septations or other suspicious features. Ascites and evidence of spread increase concern.
Hydrosalpinx.
Pyosalpinx.
Tubo-ovarian abscess.
Ectopic pregnancy involving the adnexa.

content_groups.group_title: C. Other pelvic masses that can mimic an adnexal mass

blocks.text: Pedunculated uterine fibroid.
Paraovarian or paratubal cyst.
Peritoneal inclusion cyst.
Bowel or appendiceal mass.
Pelvic kidney or other anatomical abnormality.
Exam point: Always consider pregnancy-related pathology in a woman of reproductive potential, particularly if pain or bleeding is present.

blocks.text: A postmenopausal mass is not automatically cancer, but the threshold for investigation and specialist referral is lower.
Introduce yourself and confirm the patient's identity.
Explain the purpose of the history.
Obtain consent and ensure privacy.
Ask about the patient's main concerns.
When did it begin?
Was the onset sudden or gradual?
Where is the pain located?
Is it unilateral or bilateral?
Is it constant, intermittent or colicky?
Does it radiate to the back or groin?
Is it associated with nausea or vomiting?
Is there fever or vaginal bleeding?
Sudden severe unilateral pain with nausea or vomiting raises concern for ovarian torsion.
Bloating or increasing abdominal girth.
Early satiety or reduced appetite.
Unintentional weight loss.
Constipation or altered bowel habits.
Urinary frequency or pressure symptoms.
Last menstrual period.
Cycle regularity and abnormal bleeding.
Vaginal discharge.
Dyspareunia.
Previous ovarian cysts or endometriosis.
Infertility or fertility concerns.
In reproductive-age women, ask about:
Last menstrual period.
Possibility of pregnancy.
Contraception.
Previous ectopic pregnancy.
Previous pelvic inflammatory disease or tubal surgery.
Previous pelvic or abdominal surgery.
Endometriosis or pelvic infection.
Previous malignancy.
Family history of ovarian, breast, pancreatic, prostate, colorectal or endometrial cancer.
Relevant medications, including fertility treatment and anticoagulants.
Comorbidities that may affect surgical fitness.
Menopausal status.
HRT use.
Desire for future pregnancy.
Preferences concerning ovarian preservation.
Concerns about surgical menopause if bilateral oophorectomy is being considered.
Obtain consent, provide privacy and offer a chaperone for an intimate examination.
Assess:
Vital signs and general condition.
Pallor or signs of blood loss.
Fever or signs of infection.
Weight loss or cachexia.
Respiratory distress if ascites or pleural effusion is suspected.
Inspect for distension, scars or visible masses.
Palpate for:
Mass location and approximate size.
Tenderness.
Mobility and consistency.
Ascites.
Organomegaly or peritoneal nodularity.
Percuss for ascites when appropriate and assess bowel sounds if obstruction is suspected.
With consent and a chaperone:
Inspect the cervix and vagina.
Look for bleeding or discharge.
Assess for other possible sources of symptoms.
Assess the uterus and adnexa.
Determine whether a mass is palpable.
Assess tenderness, mobility and fixation.
Note whether the mass seems separate from the uterus, while recognising that clinical examination may not reliably establish its origin.

“Abdominal examination reveals a palpable lower abdominal mass with mild tenderness. Bimanual examination suggests a right adnexal mass. The mass's precise origin and morphology cannot be determined clinically. I would arrange pelvic ultrasound and assess for features of torsion, infection or malignancy according to the clinical presentation.”
A urine or serum β-hCG test is essential in a woman of reproductive potential unless pregnancy has been reliably excluded.
If the patient has pain, bleeding or haemodynamic instability, urgently assess for ectopic pregnancy.
Transvaginal ultrasound is generally the preferred initial imaging investigation when appropriate. Transabdominal ultrasound can complement it, particularly for large masses.
Simple, unilocular cyst.
Thin, smooth wall.
No solid components or papillary projections.
No suspicious internal vascularity.
No ascites or evidence of metastatic disease.
Solid or predominantly solid mass.
Papillary projections.
Irregular thick walls or septations.
Multiple locules with suspicious features.
Strong vascularity in solid components.
Bilateral suspicious masses.
Ascites or peritoneal nodules.
Ultrasound morphology must be interpreted alongside age, symptoms and menopausal status.

blocks.text: CA-125 can be raised in benign conditions, including endometriosis, menstruation, pregnancy and pelvic inflammation. A normal result does not exclude malignancy.
MRI pelvis: useful for characterising indeterminate masses.
CT chest, abdomen and pelvis: appropriate when malignancy is suspected and staging is needed.
Doppler ultrasound: may help assess vascularity but cannot reliably rule out ovarian torsion.
Risk tools may include:
Risk of Malignancy Index (RMI).
IOTA Simple Rules.
ADNEX model.
These tools support decision-making and referral; none replaces clinical judgement or specialist review.
Management depends on symptoms, menopausal status, imaging morphology, size, growth, tumour markers and patient preferences.
Assess stability, pain, pregnancy status and ultrasound findings.
Suspected torsion, ruptured ectopic pregnancy, significant haemorrhage or sepsis: urgent assessment and treatment.
Assess malignancy risk and choose surveillance, planned surgery or specialist referral.
Appropriate for selected patients with a low-risk mass.
May include:
Reassurance after appropriate assessment.
Repeat ultrasound after an interval determined by morphology, size, menopausal status and local guidelines.
Monitoring symptoms and changes in the mass.
Clear safety-netting instructions.
Not every simple cyst requires surgery. Follow-up intervals and size thresholds vary by guideline and patient group.
Surgery may be indicated for:
Persistent or enlarging masses.
Significant symptoms.
Suspicious ultrasound features or tumour markers.
Complications such as torsion or rupture.
Diagnostic uncertainty that cannot be resolved safely with further assessment.
Options may include:
Cystectomy, preserving ovarian tissue where appropriate.
Unilateral salpingo-oophorectomy.
Bilateral salpingo-oophorectomy in selected circumstances.
Staging and cytoreductive surgery if malignancy is confirmed or strongly suspected.
For a patient with a suspicious mass, involve a gynaecological oncology team before surgery when feasible. Avoid unplanned rupture or spillage of a potentially malignant mass.
Refer promptly to gynaecological oncology.
Complete appropriate staging investigations.
Plan surgery and/or systemic therapy through the MDT.
Discuss fertility preservation where relevant and oncologically appropriate.
Offer genetic counselling and testing when indicated.
Ovarian torsion occurs when the ovary, often with the fallopian tube, twists around its supporting structures, compromising venous and lymphatic drainage and potentially arterial blood supply.
Sudden severe unilateral pelvic pain.
Nausea and vomiting.
Adnexal tenderness.
Sometimes intermittent episodes of pain from torsion and detorsion.
An ovarian mass may be present, but torsion can occur without one.
Pregnancy test.
Urgent pelvic ultrasound with Doppler as an adjunct.
Blood tests as clinically indicated.
Urgent gynaecological assessment.
Critical point: Preserved Doppler blood flow does not exclude torsion.

Suspected torsion is a gynaecological surgical emergency. Urgent laparoscopy is often required to confirm the diagnosis and detorse the adnexa. Ovarian preservation is generally favoured where feasible, especially in younger patients.
Do not delay necessary surgical assessment while waiting for a definitive ultrasound result if clinical suspicion is high.

subsections.subsection_title: Important emergency: ruptured or haemorrhagic cyst

blocks.text: A ruptured cyst may cause sudden pelvic pain and sometimes intraperitoneal bleeding.
Assess:
Vital signs and haemodynamic stability.
Severity and progression of pain.
Pregnancy status.
Haemoglobin and other tests where indicated.
Ultrasound findings and evidence of free fluid.

Stable patients with uncomplicated rupture may be managed conservatively with observation and analgesia. Haemodynamic instability or ongoing significant haemorrhage requires urgent resuscitation and surgical assessment.
Always exclude ectopic pregnancy when clinically relevant.

subsections.subsection_title: Counselling a patient with an adnexal mass

blocks.text: A good OSCE counselling response should be clear, balanced and reassuring without dismissing risk.
Explain that an adnexal mass is a finding, not a diagnosis.
Explain that many masses are benign, especially functional cysts in younger women.
Discuss the role of ultrasound and selected blood tests.
Explain why age, menopausal status and the mass's appearance matter.
Discuss surveillance or surgery if appropriate.
Explore fertility and ovarian preservation preferences.
Explain symptoms requiring urgent review.
Check understanding and invite questions.

“The scan has identified a mass near the ovary. This does not automatically mean cancer; many such masses are benign. We need to assess its appearance, your symptoms and other risk factors to decide whether monitoring or surgery is safest. If the scan shows concerning features, we will arrange specialist assessment and further investigations. I would also like to know whether preserving fertility is important to you, because that can affect the options we discuss.”
Q1. What is the first-line investigation for an adnexal mass?
Pelvic ultrasound, usually transvaginal ultrasound when appropriate, often supplemented by transabdominal imaging.
Q2. What features make an adnexal mass suspicious for malignancy?
Solid components, papillary projections, irregular thick septations, suspicious vascularity, ascites, peritoneal deposits and other evidence of spread.
Q3. Is CA-125 diagnostic of ovarian cancer?
No. It supports risk assessment but is neither sufficiently specific nor sufficiently sensitive to be used alone.
Q4. What is the RMI?
A risk assessment tool combining ultrasound features, menopausal status and CA-125 to help identify women who need specialist evaluation.
Q5. When should a patient be referred to gynaecological oncology?
When clinical assessment, ultrasound, tumour markers or risk tools suggest a significant possibility of malignancy.
Q6. What are the classic features of ovarian torsion?
Sudden unilateral pelvic pain, often with nausea and vomiting. Normal Doppler flow does not exclude the diagnosis.
Q7. Does every postmenopausal ovarian cyst require surgery?
No. Selected simple, low-risk cysts may be monitored, but management must consider symptoms, size, morphology, CA-125 where indicated and applicable guidelines.
Q8. Why is a pregnancy test important?
It helps exclude ectopic pregnancy and other pregnancy-related causes of an adnexal mass in women of reproductive potential.
Q9. Why should a suspicious mass not be casually aspirated?
Aspiration may spill malignant cells, provide inadequate diagnostic tissue and compromise definitive management.
Q10. What is the priority in suspected torsion?
Urgent gynaecological assessment and timely surgical management to preserve ovarian function where possible.

content_groups.group_title: Example: postmenopausal woman with a complex mass

blocks.text: “This is a postmenopausal woman with an adnexal mass identified on pelvic ultrasound. I would establish whether she has symptoms such as abdominal bloating, early satiety, weight loss or pain, and review her family history and relevant cancer risk factors.

“I would assess the ultrasound morphology, measure CA-125 and use an appropriate risk assessment pathway. If the mass has suspicious features or the overall risk is elevated, I would arrange prompt gynaecological oncology referral and appropriate staging imaging. If the mass is simple and low risk, surveillance may be appropriate depending on its size, symptoms and the relevant guideline.”
Failing to exclude pregnancy in a woman of reproductive potential.
Assuming a normal CA-125 excludes malignancy.
Ignoring sudden pain and vomiting in a patient with a known cyst.
Relying on Doppler flow to rule out torsion.
Recommending surgery for every simple cyst.
Failing to consider fertility preservation.
Performing unplanned aspiration or surgery on a potentially malignant mass without appropriate specialist input.

A 26-year-old woman with a known 6 cm ovarian cyst develops sudden severe right-sided pelvic pain and vomiting. Ultrasound shows an enlarged right ovary, but Doppler blood flow is still present. What is the most appropriate next step?

items: A. Discharge because preserved Doppler flow excludes torsion
B. Arrange urgent gynaecological assessment for suspected ovarian torsion
C. Repeat ultrasound in three months
D. Prescribe oral antibiotics and review in one week

blocks.text: A — Assess age, symptoms and pregnancy status.
D — Describe the mass on ultrasound.
N — Note nodules, solid components and ascites.
E — Evaluate tumour markers where indicated.
X — eXclude emergencies such as torsion and ectopic pregnancy.
A — Arrange surveillance, surgery or oncology referral according to risk.
